item.title: Korakuen Garden: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens — Guide
item.description: Korakuen, completed in 1700 for the lord of Okayama, is counted among the three great gardens of Japan alongside Kenrokuen and Kairakuen. What sets it apart is its openness: where most Japanese strolling gardens are dense and enclosed, Korakuen spreads wide lawns, ponds and streams across a river island, giving it a rare feeling of light and space. Paths wind past a working tea plantation and small rice field, teahouses, a grove of plum and cherry, and a hill you can climb for the full view — all composed around the borrowed scenery of Okayama Castle’s black keep rising beyond the garden wall.

item.title: Maruyama Park: Kyoto's Favourite Cherry-Blossom Park — Guide
item.description: Maruyama Park, tucked behind Yasaka Shrine at the foot of the Higashiyama hills, is the most popular public park in Kyoto and its most famous spot for hanami. Laid out in the Meiji era, it is a gentle landscape of ponds, streams, stone lanterns and winding paths, with tea houses and restaurants around its edges. At its heart stands a huge shidarezakura, a weeping cherry tree, which in early April is floodlit after dark and surrounded by revellers and food stalls in one of the city’s great cherry-blossom scenes.

item.title: Shukkeien Garden: A Miniature Landscape in the City — Guide
item.description: Shukkeien, whose name means ‘shrunken-scenery garden’, is a beautiful traditional strolling garden in the middle of Hiroshima, laid out in 1620 for the local lord. As its name suggests, it miniaturises whole landscapes — mountains, valleys, forests and a central pond dotted with islets — into a compact space that unfolds scene by scene as you follow the path around the water. An arched rainbow bridge crosses the pond, tea houses sit among the maples and cherries, and carp fill the water.

item.title: Tennoji Park & Keitakuen Garden: Green Heart of the South — Guide
item.description: Tennoji Park spreads beneath the towers of Abeno Harukas, a large and varied green space at the junction of the Tennoji and Shinsekai districts. Its jewel is Keitakuen, a circular strolling garden designed in the early twentieth century around a central pond, once the private garden of the Sumitomo family and a masterpiece of the period. The park also holds Osaka’s zoo, the city art museum and, at its northern edge, a modern lawn plaza lined with cafes and lit in the evening — making it a place equally suited to garden lovers, families and anyone wanting to sit down between sights.

item.title: Kinkaku-ji Guide: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion
item.description: A three-storey pavilion covered in pure gold leaf, mirrored perfectly in the still pond before it, framed by pines and — if you’re lucky — dusted with snow or backed by autumn maples: Kinkaku-ji is the postcard image of Kyoto, and one of the few sights that genuinely lives up to it. The Golden Pavilion shimmers whether under bright sun, soft cloud, or a rare winter snowfall, and the moment you round the path and it appears across the water is unforgettable.
